clue.text: I understand Greek female in charge is subject to court restriction

definitions.note: a statement made in the first person: the answer is the kind of scholar who could truthfully say it

indicators.note: whatever is subject to a restriction is held within it, so the three pieces before these words sit inside the court
a restriction confines, so the abbreviation for court closes round everything else

parts.note: Ct is the abbreviation for court, as in addresses and law reports
a lass is a girl or young woman, chiefly in Scotland and northern England
IC is the abbreviation for in charge, as in the officer i/c stores
taken as written

explanation.surface: The speaker gathers that the Greek woman who runs things has had her freedom limited by a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek female' looks like one phrase, but the definition stops at 'Greek' and is spoken by the answer. 'subject to' and 'restriction' together say the abbreviation for court hems in the other three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholar of ancient Greek and Latin could say this of themselves, so the definition is a first-person description rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Powerless to act after one, perhaps, has deposed monarch

indicators.note: to depose a ruler is to remove them from the throne, so the letters for the monarch are taken away from the longer word

parts.note: one is an example of a number, and perhaps flags that it is only an example
ER, for Elizabeth Regina, was the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: Someone is left helpless once a rival, it seems, has overthrown the king.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'one' is a usurper, but 'perhaps' marks it as only an example of the word wanted. 'has deposed' takes the monarch's royal cipher off its end; 'after' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the figurative sense: someone stunned or paralysed by shock cannot move or respond.

clue.text: Pro getting stick is to desist

indicators.note: getting means acquiring here, so the first piece has the second joined on straight after it

parts.note: pro is Latin for in favour of, which is for, as in the pros and cons
to stick something is informal British English for to put up with it, as in 'I can't stick him', which is to bear it

explanation.surface: A professional who is being criticised ought to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' joins the two pieces. To get stick is British slang for being criticised, but here 'stick' is the informal verb meaning to tolerate, as in 'I can't stick it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both verbs mean to hold back or refrain from doing something.

clue.text: Lowering of price, perhaps, making a grey area?

definitions.meaning: to shade a price is to trim it slightly; perhaps admits that odds or estimates can be trimmed the same way
darkening part of a drawing with pencil strokes or hatching, hence the question mark for the literal reading

explanation.surface: A small price cut could leave everyone unsure where they stand.
explanation.definitionFit: Trimming a price slightly and darkening part of a drawing with pencil strokes are both senses of the same verbal noun.

clue.text: Extra time needs to start with loose-limbed players

indicators.note: the piece for time needs the other two in front of it, so they open the word and it comes last

parts.note: someone loose-limbed is flexible and lithe, which is supple
the members of a team are its men, as in a side reduced to ten men
t is the abbreviation for time, as in physics formulae

explanation.surface: The added period at the end of a football match should kick off with agile athletes on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra time' is the added period that settles a drawn football match, but only 'Extra' defines. 'needs to start with' says the word begins with the other two pieces, leaving T for time at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a noun: something added on top of the usual, such as an additional charge or a newspaper's pull-out section.

clue.text: Need to pay? Audible expression of surprise

indicators.note: audible means able to be heard, so the exclamation counts by its sound and not by its spelling

parts.note: oh is what people exclaim when something surprises them

explanation.surface: Told there is a bill to settle, someone lets out a gasp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Audible' says the exclamation OH is to be heard rather than written; the answer is a verb with the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym phrase: to be in debt is to be obliged to hand over money; the question mark allows for the clipped wording.

clue.text: Certainly favoured taking action

indicators.note: taking means picking up here, so the first piece has the second added straight after it

parts.note: whatever is in is fashionable and in favour, as in the in crowd
a deed is something done, an act

explanation.surface: Someone was definitely keen on doing something about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' joins the two pieces. In the surface 'favoured' is a verb, preferred; here it is an adjective describing what is fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as an emphatic reply: both words confirm that something is undoubtedly true.

clue.text: Headline reveals millions in new careers

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for millions inside the letters that the last word turns into
new suggests the word after it is remade, its letters put into a fresh order

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged
m is the abbreviation for millions, as in a £5m deal

explanation.surface: A newspaper's front page announces that vast numbers of people are starting fresh jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges CAREERS into SCREAER, and 'in' drops M for millions inside it. 'reveals' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspaper slang: a sensational banner in huge type across the front page goes by this name.

clue.text: Composer, half-European, meets with quiet success

indicators.note: meets with means comes up against, so the shortened word is followed directly by the remaining pieces
half tells us to keep only the first three of the six letters in the word for a European

parts.note: a German is one example of a European
sh is what you say to ask for quiet
a win is a success

explanation.surface: A musician with one parent from the Continent enjoys modest acclaim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps GER, the first three letters of GERMAN, one example of a European; 'meets with' then sets the other two pieces after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: George, the American who wrote Rhapsody in Blue and Porgy and Bess.

clue.text: Maidenly characters in church — a stereotype?

indicators.note: characters are letters as well as people, and these letters sit in an unbroken run inside the three words that follow

explanation.surface: Are modest young women in the pews just a cliché?
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters in' sounds like people in a congregation, but the characters are letters: six in a row, spanning the end of 'church', the 'a' and the start of 'stereotype'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both describe the pure, virginal modesty once expected of an unmarried girl.

clue.text: A group of stars in the memory

definitions.meaning: Aries, the first sign of the zodiac, is a constellation pictured as a male sheep
a computer's working store is random-access memory, always known by its three initials

explanation.surface: A cluster of stars that someone still remembers.
explanation.definitionFit: The constellation Aries is pictured as a male sheep, and a computer's working store is known by the initials of random-access memory.

clue.text: Two-stage formula for making smart home for bird

parts.note: the word smart can be assembled in two stages, its first letter and then its last four; written out as a recipe, that is S and MART
in means at home, as in 'is anyone in?'

explanation.surface: A simple two-step recipe for building a high-tech house fit for a feathered tenant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart home' looks like one phrase, but the words part company: 'smart' is the thing being made, by the recipe S and MART, while 'home' separately gives IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a small brown-and-white member of the swallow family that nests in tunnels dug into riverbanks.

clue.text: In our time, a Bible reference disagreeable?

parts.note: AD, short for anno Domini, labels years in the present era, the one we are living in
a passage in the Bible is cited by its chapter and its verse

explanation.surface: These days, is quoting scripture thought unpleasant?
explanation.walkthrough: 'In our time' is not scene-setting: years of the present era carry the label AD, anno Domini. The question mark allows for a definition that is close rather than exact.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: unfavourable or hostile conditions are unpleasant ones, and the question mark concedes the stretch.

clue.text: A very excited Green is one looking for things to be put right

definitions.text: one looking for things to be put right

parts.note: taken as written
v is the abbreviation for very, as in v. good on a school report

indicators.note: excited letters are agitated ones, so the word straight after it is stirred into a new order

parts.note: the five letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A hugely enthusiastic environmental campaigner wants the world's wrongs fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Green' suggests an eco-politician, but 'excited' only stirs up that word's letters. The definition gently understates someone out for revenge.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphemistic description: someone seeking retribution for a wrong wants the score settled.

clue.text: Outstanding person left university given half chance

indicators.note: given means supplied with, so the two single letters have the next piece added after them

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left, as on controls marked L and R
U is the abbreviation for university, as in UCL, University College London

indicators.note: half tells us to keep only the first two of the four letters in the word for chance

parts.note: luck is chance or fortune, as in a game of chance

explanation.surface: A brilliant student would quit college at the slightest opportunity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given' adds the last piece and 'half' keeps LU, the first two letters of LUCK. In the surface 'left' is a verb, departed; here it is only the abbreviation L.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang, originally American: a remarkable or wonderful example of its kind, whether an object or a human being.

clue.text: This person's to appear in a commercial? Express censure

indicators.note: appearing in something means being found inside it, so the setter's contraction goes within the phrase for a commercial

parts.note: a television commercial is an advert, and the article comes along too: an advert
this person is the setter speaking, so this person's, short for this person is, becomes I'm

explanation.surface: Is the speaker really going to feature in a TV advertisement? Make your disapproval known.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks whether the speaker will feature on television; in fact 'This person's' is the setter saying 'I am' in contracted form, and 'to appear in' places it inside the two-word phrase for 'a commercial', article included.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the verb means to pass critical comment or find fault, and is usually followed by 'on'.

clue.text: Softly, softly? Certainly not when copper's on beat

indicators.note: in a down clue on means on top of, so the symbol for copper is written above the other piece

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper; the 's is short for is
softly twice over would be pp, pianissimo, in a musical score; certainly not asks for its opposite instead, ff, fortissimo, very loud

explanation.surface: A gentle approach? Hardly, when a police officer is out on patrol.
explanation.walkthrough: A copper on the beat is a British policeman on patrol, and Softly, Softly was a British police drama. 'on' stacks CU above FF: 'softly, softly' is pp in music, and 'Certainly not' replaces it with its loud opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to strike someone with the open hand, especially about the head.

clue.text: A good lot of drinks gets one lying on the bed

parts.note: taken as written
g is the abbreviation for good, as in vg on a marked essay
in a pub, the set of drinks one person buys for everyone in the group is called a round

explanation.surface: After plenty of alcohol, someone ends up flat out on the mattress.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is not a mattress but the floor of the sea or a river, where a stranded ship rests. In a pub, the set of drinks one person buys for the whole group is a round.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: a stranded ship rests on the floor of the sea or a river.

clue.text: Horse a cheerless pet when out of sorts

indicators.note: out of sorts means unwell or disordered, so the three words before it, once put out of order, make something new

parts.note: all thirteen letters, the article included, are the ones to rearrange

explanation.surface: A horse makes a gloomy companion animal when it is feeling unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when out of sorts' rearranges all thirteen letters of A CHEERLESS PET, article included, into a horse that races over fences and ditches.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a racehorse that runs over a course of fences, hedges and water jumps.

clue.text: Going after baddies, the journalist used foul language

indicators.note: going after fixes the order: the piece for the journalist follows the piece for the baddies

parts.note: curs are contemptible people, scoundrels, as well as mongrel dogs
ed is short for editor, the journalist who runs a newspaper

explanation.surface: A reporter chasing villains swore along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going after' sounds like a reporter pursuing villains, but it only fixes the order: ED, short for editor, follows the word for scoundrels.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: swore or uttered profanities, in the past tense like the definition.

clue.text: Coin from South Eastern Crete's different

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation for south-east or south-eastern

indicators.note: different tells us the word before it, final s and all, has its letters put in another order

parts.note: all six letters are rearranged, the s of the possessive included

explanation.surface: The money used in one corner of a Greek island is unlike that anywhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive s counts: 'different' rearranges all six letters of 'Crete's', while the compass abbreviation stands untouched in front. The coin is ancient Roman rather than Greek, and 'from' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: an ancient Roman coin, originally silver, worth a quarter of a denarius.

clue.text: Higher-education type maybe in college blazer etc.?

parts.note: uni is the everyday British shortening of university, where higher education takes place
a form of something is a type or kind of it

explanation.surface: A university student might be seen wearing the college jacket and all that goes with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one picture of a student in a blazer, a smart jacket in school or college colours. In fact the first two words give the pieces and 'maybe in' merely links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a blazer and matching tie are the prescribed outfit every pupil wears, and the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Anti-bigotry is seen to be so generous

parts.note: ignoring the hyphen, the middle three of these eleven letters spell BIG, so the word has BIG at its heart

explanation.surface: Opposing prejudice is regarded as a very kind and giving thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer describes the first word: ignore the hyphen and the middle three of its eleven letters spell BIG. 'is seen to be so' says the word visibly has that property.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both describe someone kind and giving, who shares freely with others.

clue.text: In a most difficult situation, where pencil meets paper?

definitions.meaning: the idiom for being where the danger or pressure is greatest, like soldiers in the front line
taken literally: the pointed tip is the only part of a pencil that touches the page

explanation.surface: Someone is in dire trouble at the very moment of putting pencil to paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the place of greatest danger or pressure, and literally the pointed tip of a pencil touching the page.

clue.text: One's quick going under

parts.note: quick is a noun here, the tender living flesh, as in bitten to the quick; 's is short for has, so this is a thing with that flesh running beneath it

explanation.surface: Somebody sinks, or falls asleep under anaesthetic, in no time at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests somebody sinking or failing fast. Read the apostrophe-s as 'has' and 'quick' as a noun, the sensitive flesh, and the clue describes the hard plate lying over it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: the quick is the tender flesh at the tip of a digit, and it lies beneath this horny plate.

clue.text: An alien's unusual, with name using botanist's classification

indicators.note: with means accompanied by, so the letter for name is added after the rearranged letters
unusual tells us the first two words, less the apostrophe s, appear in an unfamiliar order

parts.note: the seven letters of an and alien are rearranged; the 's only stands for is
n is the abbreviation for name, as on forms and in reference books

explanation.surface: A strange visitor from another planet goes by a name in a plant scientist's Latin system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges AN ALIEN into LINNAEA, and 'with' adds N for name. The botanist is Carl Linnaeus, the Swede who devised the two-part Latin naming of species.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective for anything following the system of Carl Linnaeus, the Swedish botanist who gave species two-part Latin names.

clue.text: Transfer from room outside English cricket ground

indicators.note: outside tells us the abbreviation for room goes round the letter for English

parts.note: rm is the abbreviation for room, as in property adverts
E is the abbreviation for English, as in OED, the Oxford English Dictionary
The Oval is a cricket ground in south London, home of Surrey and a regular England Test venue

explanation.surface: Someone is moved out of a space just beyond an English cricket venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps RM round E. The cricket ground is The Oval in south London, home of Surrey; 'English' belongs to the wordplay, not to the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a noun: the moving of something from one place to another, as when a household's furniture is shifted.

clue.text: Building material one found outside hospital

indicators.note: found outside tells us the word for one is placed round the letter for hospital

parts.note: single means one, as in a single ticket or not a single mistake
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs and maps

explanation.surface: Somebody came across construction supplies lying in the hospital grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found outside' wraps SINGLE round H. In the surface 'one' is somebody making a discovery; here it is simply the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a thin wooden or asphalt tile laid in overlapping rows to cover a roof or wall.

clue.text: Preserve tree, having brought in business expert

indicators.note: having brought in means having taken inside, so the tree's name holds the letters for the business expert

parts.note: an elm is a tall deciduous tree
an MBA is someone holding the degree of Master of Business Administration

explanation.surface: Save a tree by hiring a management consultant.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about saving a tree with a consultant's help, but this preserving is done to a corpse. 'having brought in' means the tree's name takes the business degree inside it; holders of that degree are known by its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym for treating a dead body with chemicals so that it does not decay.

clue.text: Troublesome youngster runs into club

indicators.note: into tells us the letter for runs goes inside the word for club

parts.note: a bat is a club for striking a ball, as in cricket or baseball
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A badly behaved child dashes into a nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts R, the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs, inside BAT. In the surface 'runs' is a verb and the club a nightclub.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a badly behaved, spoilt child.
